title: EXAMINING THE IMPACT OF DIGITALIZATION AND INEQUALITY POST COVID -19 IN AFRICA
abstract: The impact of the coronavirus (Covid-19) has changed economic, social, political life around the world. One of the most significant effects of the pandemic has been the accelerated adoption of digital technologies in many sectors of the global economy. The pandemic has thrust the world into a situation where people without access are completely excluded. Therefore, this study investigated impacts of Covid 19 in Africa. The analysis is based on the systematic review of secondary data on Covid 19 in Africa. This reflects the preference for living alone during pandemic in least developed country (ITU,2019). In low and middle –income countries the number of women who own a mobile phone is 10% less than men, and the number of women using mobile internet worldwide is less than 300 million (GSMA,2020). The literature in this article will fill the knowledge gap on how to conceptualise the relationship between digital inclusion and rising inequality in Africa. title: Editorial Note
abstract: Faculty of Humanities Teaching and Learning Colloquium 2025 (T&L Colloquium 25) hosted by the Faculty of Humanities, North-West University, South Africa took place in Rustenburg, South Africa, from September 9-11, 2025, with a rich and stimulating programme filled with inspiring keynotes, contributed papers, workshops and panels. This bi-annual colloquium brings together educators, researchers, students, policymakers, and community practitioners. The main theme of T&L Colloquium 25 was “Reimagining the Future of Humanities Knowledge and Pedagogy: Decoloniality, Technology and the Social Justice Imperative.” This special issue of the Journal of Contemporary Society And Education (JCSE contains Thirteen (13) selected papers presented at T&L Colloquium 2025. Selected contributions come from within and outside of South Africa and address a wide range of issues in humanities, decoloniality, technology and the social justice.

title: THE OMITTED CONVERSATION: INCORPORATING TEACHER UNIONSCHOLARSHIP FOR A TRANSFORMATIVE EDUCATIONAL AGENDA WITHIN THE EDUCATIONAL LANDSCAPE IN SOUTH AFRICA
abstract: The global paradigm shift in educational transformation necessitates a reappraisal of the roles assumed by all relevant stakeholders in education, including teacher unions. Teacher unions have historically been situated within the realms of labour advocacy, engaging in the bargaining process and striving for improved working conditions for educators. However, teacher unions have been marginalized in discussions regarding long-term educational reform, as they lack representation in both school governance structures and professional management roles. This study examines the overlooked discussions surrounding the incorporation of teacher unions into school leadership structures. This study critically examines the overarching narratives surrounding educational innovation through the lens of institutional theory. This study presents a compelling argument on a global scale, asserting that teacher unions are not merely reactive entities. Instead, they hold transformative potential to reshape educational landscapes by advocating for policies that promote social equity, democratic participation, and professional development. title: EXAMINING FACTORS BEHIND INSTITUTIONAL ACHIEVEMENT: A SCENARIO OF SECONDARY SCHOOLS IN LIMPOPO PROVINCE
abstract: This paper explores a host of factors in secondary schools that earn for an educational institution a label of being an achieving school from the perspective of teachers serving in the School Governing Body and the Representative Council of Learners. The paper was motivated by diverse discourses about learner-achievement, most of which are mainly based on the perspective of professional teachers. This paper is conceptual and empirical in nature within the qualitative research paradigm. The question guiding this paper is: what are the host of factors in secondary schools that earn for an educational institution a label of being an achieving school from the perspective of teachers serving in the School Governing Body and the Representative Council of Learners? Narrative enquiry and interviewing techniques were used to collect data. Out of the population of 15 secondary schools in one of the circuits in Vhembe district in Limpopo Province, South Africa, twelve schools were conveniently sampled. title: DECOLONISING DIGITAL HEALTH PROMOTION IN AFRICAN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS: A JUSTICE-ORIENTED LITERATURE REVIEW
abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly central to higher education globally, yet their integration into health promotion in African higher education institutions (HEIs) often reproduces structural, cultural, and epistemic inequalities. While digitalisation has expanded access to health education, it remains shaped by colonial legacies, linguistic hierarchies, and externally controlled technological infrastructures. This conceptual paper develops a Digital Health Justice Framework to address these challenges and guide equitable and culturally responsive digital health promotion in African HEIs. Drawing on a critical synthesis of four key elements, literature, digitalisation, health promotion, equity, and digital divides, Critical Digital Pedagogy (CDP) and Decolonial Theory, the paper integrates micro-level pedagogical approaches with macro-structural analyses. Five interrelated pillars are articulated: inclusive access, culturally responsive pedagogy and linguistic justice, epistemic plurality, participatory co-design, and digital sovereignty. title: POPULATION ETHICS AND ITS IMPLICATION FOR DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
abstract: This paper discusses population ethics and the implication for developing countries. Population ethics examines our moral obligations to future generations, particularly when evaluating choices that impact many generations to come. Unfortunately, both empirical climate science and moral philosophy yield concerning findings. Developing a theory that outlines our moral duties to future generations has proven challenges, and classical moral and political philosophies often lead to counterintuitive conclusions. This study adopted a qualitative research method, leveraging descriptive and analytical tools to examine existing literature on population ethics. Primary and secondary sources were consulted, including philosophical texts, policy documents, and case studies, to provide a comprehensive understanding of the topic. By understanding the ethical implications of population trends, policymakers can make more informed decisions that balance the needs of current and future generations, ultimately fostering a more sustainable and equitable future. title: EVALUATING THE USE OF QR CODES AS A TOOL OF ASSESSMENT IN TEACHING AND LEARNING WITHIN HIGHER EDUCATION BLENDED LEARNING
abstract: This paper explores the use of QR (Quick Response) codes as an innovative tool for assessment in educational environments. The research was guided by the following key questions: (1) What are the advantages of using QR codes as an assessment method in teaching and learning? (2) How effective are QR codes in supporting assessment practices? The study was carried out with third-year education students enrolled in the Literacies in Education module. From a group of 1,500 students, a purposive sample of 29 participants completed an online questionnaire consisting of nine items aimed at exploring students’ perceptions of mobile learning and the use of QR codes for assessment. This paper employed a qualitative research approach and adopted an interpretivist paradigm. The results reveal a range of student perceptions. While descriptions of mobile learning varied, the majority of participants recognised the potential of QR codes as an assessment tool. Approximately 48.3% indicated that they would likely incorporate QR codes into their future teaching practices. title: POLICY WINDOWS AND MISSED OPPORTUNITIES: RETHINKING TEACHERUNION AGENCY IN POST-COVID SCHOOL LEADERSHIP AND GOVERNANCE REFORM
abstract: Teacher unions hold a vital and debated role in the governance and professional management of schools in South Africa. Public discourse often characterizes unions as either obstructive or protective labor entities; however, there is a scarcity of empirical research regarding their institutional roles within school leadership frameworks, especially in the context of post-COVID-19 reforms. This study analyses the role of teacher unions as institutional stakeholders in school governance, their strategic positioning during reform and crisis, and their mediation between policy frameworks and pedagogical practice.The study employed a qualitative interpretive design, informed by an institutional perspective on organizational legitimacy and temporal alignment. Semi-structured interviews were carried out with twelve participants, including four principals, four members of the School Management Team (SMT), and four union representatives. title: ASSESSING THE ROLE OF THE COVID-19 CATCH-UP RECOVERY PROGRAMME ON LEARNER PERFORMANCE IN EFAL
abstract: This study investigates the influence of the COVID-19 Curriculum Recovery Plan (CRP) on the academic performance of English First Additional Language (EFAL) learners in the Vhembe District, Limpopo Province, South Africa. The CRP was introduced to mitigate the severe learning disruptions caused by school closures during the pandemic. Adopting a qualitative phenomenological design informed by social constructivism, the study explored the lived experiences of educators and learners across four secondary schools in the Nzhelele Central Circuit. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with three categories of participants, providing first-hand insights into the implementation process of the CRP. Findings reveal that while the CRP generated some positive outcomes, such as enhanced learner engagement, targeted curricular adjustments, professional development for teachers, and improved Grade 12 achievement, it was undermined by systemic challenges. Chief among these were limited digital access, inadequate teacher capacity for online pedagogy, and fragile institutional support mechanisms. title: MITIGATING GRAMMATICAL AMBIGUITY IN ENGLISHPREPOSITIONAL PHRASES AT DZINDI CIRCUIT SECONDARY SCHOOL,SOUTH AFRICA
abstract: Even though tenses are an essential component of the English language, tense substitution poses a significant challenge for non-native English speakers. This study investigated a strategy to mitigate grammatical ambiguity in English prepositional phrases at Dzindi Circuit Secondary School, South Africa. Grounded by Noam Chomsky’s Transformational Generative Grammar and Oyinlola's Contrastive Analysis Hypothesis, this study adopted a qualitative approach to obtain an in-depth understanding of the phenomenon. The study population consisted of 99 Grade 11 English First Additional Language (FAL) learners in the 2025 academic year. Sixteen (16) learners were randomly selected for this study. Data were collected using a closed-ended questionnaire, as it provides predetermined responses to facilitate informed decision-making. They were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 29, due to its new interpretative enhancements. title: ENTREPRENEURIAL EDUCATION AND SUSTAINABLE ENTREPRENEURSHIP ADVANCING SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENTGOALS IN SOUTH AFRICA THROUGH SMALL BUSINESSES
abstract: The alignment of entrepreneurial education with sustainable entrepreneurship has become increasingly important as countries pursue the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In South Africa, small businesses play a critical role in economic development yet face structural barriers that limit their adoption of sustainable practices. This study examined how entrepreneurial education influences the capacity of small businesses to align with and advance the SDGs. A desktop research design was employed, drawing on peer-reviewed literature, policy reports, and documented case studies. The findings indicate that South African university programs that embed sustainability into entrepreneurship curricula (particularly through experiential learning and innovation hubs) enhance graduates’ ability to establish SDG-aligned ventures. Evidence from initiatives at the University of Cape Town Graduate School of Business, the University of the Western Cape, and Stellenbosch University’s LaunchLab demonstrates that sustainability-integrated programs contribute to ventures in renewable energy, waste management, sustainable agriculture, and circular production models. title: EMERGING CAREER PATHWAYS FOR HUMANITIES GRADUATES: INTEGRATING WELL BEING AND SUSTAINABILITY
abstract: In an era marked by complex global challenges, the intersection of humanities education and employability demands renewed attention. This paper investigates emerging career pathways that foreground wellbeing and sustainable development, positioning humanities graduates as key contributors to sustainable and ethical futures. Drawing on interdisciplinary scholarship, the study elucidates how competencies cultivated through the humanities such as critical thinking, ethical reflection, and cultural literacy equip individuals to navigate and address pressing social and environmental issues. By situating employability within the frameworks of wellbeing and sustainability, the research identifies novel professional opportunities in sectors including community engagement, policy development, and social innovation. The findings advocate for an expanded employability paradigm that integrates humanistic knowledge with sustainable development goals, underscoring the vital role of humanities disciplines in shaping resilient, inclusive societies.

title: ANALYZING THE EFFECT OF THE DISCONNECTION BETWEEN THE CURRICULUM AND AFRICA’S INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE ON EFFECTIVE LEARNING
abstract: One of the purported legacies of colonialism is the imposition of the Western education curriculum bequeathed to Africa. This curriculum was deceptively imposed on Africa in a bid to repudiate Africa’s originality and belittle its authentic experiences and indigenous knowledge. With this, the European psyche was superimposed on that of Africa, thus relegating its indigenous knowledge system. This has had severe implications for effective learning in Africa. Although studies have been conducted to decolonize the Western curriculum bequeathed to Africa, without the deployment of the mechanism of African indigenous knowledge. The main objective of this paper is to examine the implications of the disconnect between the Western curriculum and Africa’s indigenous knowledge on effective learning in African higher institutions of learning. This paper, through the use of desktop document analysis, argues that effective learning that can effectively solve most of Africa’s problems largely depends on incorporation of AIK into school curricula. title: EXPLORING THE USAGE OF METADISCOURSE IN A RESEARCH PROPOSALWRITTEN BY HONOURS STUDENTS FROM A SELECTED UNIVERSITY
abstract: Academic writing is not only about presenting information and research findings but also about guiding readers through arguments and engaging them in the text. One important linguistic resource that helps writers achieve this is Metadiscourse. Hence, this paper explored the usage of Metadiscourse in research proposals by university students. Both qualitative and quantitative design methods were used. The students’ proposals served as a data-collection instrument. The participants were 10 university students. The results show that the students used both interactive and interactional Metadiscourse in their research proposals to guide readers through their arguments and enhance overall clarity. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of Metadiscourse in academic writing, particularly in research proposals, as a means to facilitate understanding and foster connections between the writer and the reader.

title: FAKE NEWS, ELECTORAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE ROLE OF ARTIFCIAL INTELLIGENCE IN NIGERIA
abstract: One of thebiggest challenges confronting Nigeria since the restoration of democratic rule in 1999 is how to deliver a free, fair and transparent electoral contest acceptable to all and sundry. Closely related to this is how incidence of fake news otherwise referredto as misinformation continues to undermine electoral administration in Nigeria. With the purveyors of fake news deliberately undermining elections, it is yet to be seen how INEC can earn the trust and confidence of Nigerians on this important assignment.The objective of this paper is to examine how the incidence of fake news sabotages electoral administration in Nigeria and what needs to be done to improve the process. The paper adopts a thematic approach with heavy reliance on secondary sources to arrive at its conclusion. To achieve its objective, the paper is anchored on systems theory as a basis of analysis, interpretation and conclusion. The paper concludes that electoral administration was largely undermined by fake news hence, the need to deal withfake news and misinformation.
